candidates.mundane_alternative: A07 — a pioneering 1947 commercial microwave terminal, architecturally notable, which like most surviving microwave real estate carried government traffic under contract during the Cold War and is now a cell site. WHAT WOULD DISTINGUISH IT from something more: nothing found suggests anything more about the building. The interesting object here is not the building but the NETWORK, and the register should be careful not to let an architecturally distinctive tower stand in for a system it merely touched.
candidates.claim_origin: Three genuinely separate origins, which is unusual for this beat. (1) The architectural and historical record originates with the heritage documentation — DC Historic Sites / DC Preservation League and, behind it, the NRHP nomination, plus Tenleytown local history material. (2) The scholarly account of Western Union's microwave network originates with David S. Rotenstein, 'Towers for Telegrams', IA: The Journal of the Society for Industrial Archeology 32(2), 2006, with related material on his blog (historian4hire) including a Western Union microwave network survey and a 2010 piece on continuity-of-government sites as recent-past resources. (3) The WAWS material and the node list originate with Albert LaFrance, coldwar-c4i.net. These three do not descend from one another.
candidates.expected_records: NRHP NOMINATION — X3 and reachable through NPS; the single highest-value document for this candidate and a genuine T1/T2 primary. DC HISTORIC PRESERVATION OFFICE landmark file — X3. DC RECORDER OF DEEDS — X3, universal floor. FCC ASR AND ULS — X3, ownership and licence history for a registered structure in continuous commercial use. DCA/DISA AND DoD DOCUMENTATION MENTIONING 'WAWS' — X1 to X2 and completely unexplored; a system with an acronym and a node list including NSA and AJCC endpoints should leave traces in GovInfo, DTIC and NARA finding aids. WESTERN UNION CORPORATE RECORDS — X2; Rotenstein evidently reached some. MILCON — X0, Western Union is not an appropriated entity, which is the Mount Pony blind-spot pattern exactly and should be flagged on the entry.
candidates.confidence_note: I am including this candidate less for the tower than for WAWS. The register's Long Lines material will be AT&T-shaped by default because that is where the enthusiast literature is; Western Union ran a parallel hardened government network that is barely represented anywhere, has a named acronym that will index well, and has a serious scholarly treatment already in print. If one thread from this sweep is worth a dedicated follow-up cycle, it is this one.

propositions.statement: A 1945–47 cast-concrete microwave terminal building with an attached octagonal tower, approximately 73 feet tall, exists at the site.
propositions.assessment: This is the only candidate on the beat with a plausible route to a genuine T1 primary: the building and tower are reported listed on the National Register of Historic Places and are carried by DC Historic Sites (DC Preservation League). An NRHP nomination is a T1/T2 document, machine-resolvable through NPS, that describes construction, dimensions, materials, architect and history on its face. Conditional: A on the nomination alone, once reachable. This is also the only candidate where the architect is named — Leon Chatelain Jr. — which opens an architectural-records lineage entirely independent of the Cold War literature.
supporting: DC Historic Sites (DC Preservation League) entry — 73-foot octagonal transmission tower built 1945–1947 near the city's highest elevation, designed by Leon Chatelain Jr.

propositions.statement: The tower served as a node in Western Union's Washington Area Wideband System, a Department of Defense redundant data and video network of coaxial and 6 GHz microwave links, connecting facilities including the Naval Security Station, NSA's Friendship Annex, Andrews AFB, Liberty Dam, and the Alternate Joint Communications Center at Blue Ridge Summit.
propositions.assessment: This is the most valuable and least-known thing I found on this beat. WAWS is a named, acronymed DoD system with a documented node list, and it is a Western Union rather than AT&T network — a whole hardened-communications lineage largely absent from the Long Lines-dominated literature. Its endpoints are named, acknowledged federal installations, which makes the topology checkable. The claim originates with LaFrance's WAWS pages and route map. Conditional: WAWS as a PROGRAM is a strong candidate for B or better once DoD/DCA documentation is searched, because unlike 'Project Offices' it has an acronym that will appear in indexes.
supporting: coldwar-c4i.net WAWS index and WAWS microwave route map
coldwar-c4i.net Tenleytown page — repurposed in the late 1970s as a WAWS repeater
Rotenstein 2006 on Western Union's national-security communications role
undercutting: The Tenleytown building itself is an above-ground 1947 commercial structure and nothing suggests it was hardened. A node in a defence network is not thereby a bunker, and this candidate is included as a comms-relay, not as a hardened facility.
propositions.proposed_band: X
propositions.diagnosticity_note: A named system acronym is disproportionately diagnostic in this domain because it is a search key that reaches indexed federal corpora. 'WAWS' is the kind of term that appears in DCA/DISA histories, in GAO reports and in appropriations language, where 'Project Office' does not. The highest-value follow-up on this entire beat may be a systematic WAWS search across GovInfo, DTIC and NARA.

propositions.statement: The Tenleytown terminal was hardened beyond ordinary construction.
propositions.assessment: No source claims this and I am recording the proposition specifically in order to record its absence. A cast-concrete 1947 building near a city's high point is a microwave terminal, not a bunker, and the register should hold a node of a national-security network at D or below on hardening unless something says otherwise. Conditional: this is a case where an expected record IS informative — an NRHP nomination describes construction in detail, so a nomination that does not mention protective engineering is a genuine, if mild, UNDERCUTS row rather than a silence.
undercutting: An NRHP nomination, if it resolves, would be a detailed architectural description by a party with authority over the historic record; its silence on hardening would be informative in a way most silences on this beat are not.
propositions.proposed_band: X
propositions.diagnosticity_note: This row exists to make a point the beat needs: participation in a defence network is not hardening, and the two propositions must not be allowed to borrow from each other. The Tenleytown tower is a case where FUNCTION is interesting and HARDEN is almost certainly negative.

propositions.assessment: Reported consistently and a priori highly plausible for a 1957-58 SAC numbered-air-force combat operations centre — this is precisely the facility class for which blast hardening was standard and funded. But 'hardened to protect it from the effects of a nearby nuclear blast' is narrative phrasing with no standard, overpressure or closure specification behind it in anything reaching me. Plausibility from facility class is a base-rate argument and BES deliberately keeps base rate out of the arithmetic.

PACCS as a system is independently documented in Air Force literature. The strongest route here is AFHRA unit histories, which are indexed by IRIS number and which describe facilities directly — an unusually favourable and underused channel for this candidate.

propositions.statement: SEPARATE AND MUCH WEAKER CLAIM, GRADED APART: the Federal Reserve stored a large quantity of currency at the facility for post-attack economic reconstitution.
propositions.assessment: I have split this from the records-storage claim deliberately, because they are being carried together and they do not deserve the same treatment. The records-storage claim is unremarkable and probably true. The CURRENCY claim is hedged in the sources themselves — one states 'Allegedly they stored large sums of money there as well' — and it is a textbook transposition candidate: the documented American post-attack currency site is the Federal Reserve's Mount Pony facility at Culpeper, Virginia, which held shrink-wrapped currency for monetary reconstitution from 1969 to 1988 and is a calibration case in this project's own suite. A currency-reconstitution story attaching itself to a second, unrelated Federal Reserve-occupied bunker in the same period is exactly what transposition looks like. I am NOT asserting the transposition — I am naming it as the leading alternative and the thing to test.
propositions.proposed_band: X (and I would expect this to resolve as unsupported or as transposed from Mount Pony)
undercutting: The sources carrying the claim hedge it explicitly with 'allegedly', which is the carriers themselves declining to vouch for it.

propositions.diagnosticity_note: The discriminating record exists and is reachable in principle: FRASER, the St Louis Fed's archival platform, exposes Federal Reserve Record Group 82 including a Boston series at Box 2644, and Boston is the correct district for Hadley. A finding-aid hit naming the Notch would settle the records-storage claim and possibly the currency claim; its absence would be weakly informative, since Federal Reserve facility records are not comprehensively public. Note that the Federal Reserve is non-appropriated: no MILCON line, no FRPP entry, no FPDS record and no GSA disposal will ever exist for a Fed facility, so those four profiles are X0 and their silence carries nothing. That is the Mount Pony blind-spot lesson applying a second time.

propositions.statement: These sites are hardened facilities.
propositions.assessment: This proposition is stated in order to be answered NO, and that is the entry's purpose. These are unmanned repeater huts — small buildings on rural land with a tower, built to relay telephone and television traffic. Nothing in the source material claims hardening for them. The great majority of the several hundred Long Lines sites in the United States are of this class, not of the Lyons or Fairview class, and a register that ingests the Long Lines corpus without that distinction will manufacture hundreds of spurious hardened facilities out of ordinary telephone plant. Conditional: this proposition should grade at F or R, not at D — there is no admissible support and, unlike a classified facility, the silence here IS informative, because an unmanned rural repeater has no expected-record profile that would conceal hardening.

Over a hundred main stations were hardened; roughly a thousand repeater vaults were built to a much lower standard; and the unmanned microwave repeaters were not hardened at all. Three tiers, one corpus, one name. Every hardening claim must be attached to a specific site's specific class, and the popular literature routinely attaches the main-station specifications to whatever site it happens to be describing.

location.description: The research programme is located at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory, New Mexico. The claimed transcontinental network has no location and never has had one - no source in the lineage gives a portal, an alignment, or a coordinate.
location.basis: The programme is institutionally located by its report series. The claimed network is non-located in the BES 10.4 sense - documented as a claim, coordinates genuinely never asserted. No coordinate invented.

lineage.assessment: TWO LINEAGES THAT MUST NOT BE MERGED. (A) The DOCUMENT lineage — OSTI LA-5354-MS, OSTI LA-4547, US Patent 3,693,731, the DRI/DOE U12t tunnel evaluation — is institutional and genuinely independent by the access test: LASL, the AEC and NSF each recorded their own programme for their own purposes. FOUR independent roots. (B) The NETWORK-INFERENCE lineage is a single 1990s fringe-book cluster: Sauder 1995 moving from 'the government studied deep basing and rock-melting' to 'therefore deep bases and tunnels were built', with Schneider supplying the numbers. ONE root.
lineage.collapse_or_note: A register that lets (A) launder (B) has performed citogenesis on itself — the Sauder-as-bibliography trap the calibration suite flags at F-03. Note the self-sealing structure: the 1972 patent's own stated advantage is that the process produces no muck or tailings, and that is deployed downstream to explain why the most diagnostic possible signal is missing. A claim engineered so the absence of its strongest disconfirming signal counts as support has removed its own falsifiability.

propositions.statement: A US government research programme to develop a nuclear-powered rock-melting tunnelling machine (the 'subterrene') was proposed, funded and prosecuted at Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory in the early 1970s, and was cancelled without a full-scale prototype.
propositions.assessment: This is the strongest 'the fringe was sitting on real documents' case I found, and it is why the beat brief's warning against assuming falsity matters. Search results surface machine-resolvable identifiers of exactly the class BES treats as D4-capable: LA-5354-MS, 'Systems and Cost Analysis for a Nuclear Subterrene Tunneling Machine: A Preliminary Study', J. H. Altseimer, Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory informal report, September 1973, sponsored in part by NSF RANN, with an OSTI DOI of 10.2172/4444905 and a UNT Digital Library ark of 67531/metadc1033181; an earlier LA-4547, 'A Preliminary Study of the Nuclear Subterrene'; and US Patent 3,693,731, issued 26 September 1972 to Armstrong, McInteer, Mills and Potter, assigned to the US Atomic Energy Commission, for a method and apparatus for tunnelling by melting. I resolved NONE of these. I am recording identifiers that appeared in search-result titles and snippets from OSTI, UNT, INIS and patent aggregators - which is materially better than an identifier I generated, and materially worse than a document. The register should treat them as leads and queue them.

propositions.statement: A network of tunnels constructed by nuclear subterrene technology connects US military and government installations.
propositions.assessment: Nothing supports this and the programme record cuts against it. The inferential move the fringe corpus makes here is visible and nameable: from 'the AEC patented a rock-melting tunneller' to 'therefore a national tunnel network was melted', with no intervening evidence. Sauder makes this move explicitly and it is the single most instructive error in the corpus, because the first half is genuinely documented and the second half is not documented at all. Worse for the claim: the 1972 patent's own stated advantage - that the process produces no muck or tailings - is used downstream as the explanation for why no spoil exists, which converts the absence of the most diagnostic possible signal into apparent support. That is a claim structured to be unfalsifiable, and BES should say so rather than merely score it low.

The shaft is the only physical object in this entry and it is the register's 'the hole is certain, the function is not' case in almost pure form - except that here even the hole is only newspaper-attested.

propositions.statement: The claim originates in a notarised affidavit by Earl Dorr, executed in Pasadena on 16 November 1934, first published in the California Mining Journal, November 1940.
propositions.assessment: Unusually well-specified for a fringe origin, and unusually testable. Search summaries give a notarisation date and place, a publication date and venue six years later, and - importantly - report that at least two versions of the affidavit circulate, one bearing a 10 December 1934 notarisation and claimed by its holder to be the original. Competing versions of a foundational document are a textual-criticism problem, not a rumour problem, and they are resolvable: a notarised instrument leaves a notary journal entry, and the California Mining Journal is a physical serial. The most diagnostic detail I found is negative and cuts against the whole downstream tradition: the affidavit reportedly does not mention Kokoweef Peak, Crystal Cave, or the Peysert brothers at all. If that holds, then the specific location and the Native American provenance story are LATER accretions attached to Dorr's text, not content of it - which is the classic backsourcing result.
propositions.proposed_band: X - VERIFICATION PENDING. Ceiling if the November 1940 California Mining Journal issue resolves and both affidavit variants are collated: A. The variant problem means the honest ceiling on 'what the affidavit says' is lower than on 'that an affidavit exists'.
supporting: The Mojave Project, 'Kokoweef: Still Searching for the Lost River of Gold' - a documentary field project with a dispatch on the site, reporting the 16 November 1934 Pasadena notarisation, the November 1940 California Mining Journal publication, the two-variant problem, and the absence of Kokoweef, Crystal Cave and the Peyserts from the affidavit text (search snippet only)
PBS SoCal Artbound, 'Still Searching for the Mojave's Lost River of Gold' (search snippet only)
kokoweefinc.net, 'The Legend from Earl Dorr' - the operator's own hosting of the text, which is a party to the claim (search snippet only)
undercutting: The existence of two notarised variants is itself an UNDERCUTS row against any claim about what the affidavit says, though not against its existence
propositions.diagnosticity_note: A notarised instrument with a date and a notary is a genuinely discriminating artifact for ORIGIN: it fixes a terminus ante quem in a public-facing legal form and it can be checked. The accretion finding - Kokoweef, Crystal Cave and the Peyserts absent from the source text but universal downstream - is the single most diagnostic thing available on this entry, because a later tradition that adds specifics the source lacks is descent, not corroboration.

propositions.statement: A cave system exists beneath Kokoweef Peak.
propositions.assessment: Apparently true and mundane. Crystal Cave and adjacent caves under Kokoweef are described in summaries as real and verified, and Dorr is reported to have genuinely explored them before 1934. The register's characteristic split applies exactly: the hole is (probably) certain, the function is not.
propositions.proposed_band: X - VERIFICATION PENDING. Ceiling if the MRDS/USMIN/California mine-records entries and the BLM claim record resolve: A. Note that BES treats MSHA/BLM regulated-mine records as UNDERCUTS at minus D1 for any HARDEN or concealed-facility reading while supporting EXIST - one artifact, opposite signs on two propositions.
supporting: Multiple summaries describing verified caves beneath Kokoweef, including Crystal Cavern (search snippets only)
BLM lode claim 'RAINBOW', 20.66 acres, San Bernardino County, located 2007, held by Kokoweef Inc., surfaced via thediggings.com (a T4 mirror of BLM MLRS; the underlying BLM record was not resolved)
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Cave existence is D0 for the gold-river claim - a limestone peak in the Mojave producing solution caves is exactly what the geology predicts with or without a river of gold.

propositions.statement: A cavern system approximately 3000 feet deep containing a flowing underground river over gold-bearing black sands exists beneath Kokoweef Peak.
propositions.assessment: This is the entry that most repays the register's insistence that absence is only evidence where presence is expected - because here it emphatically is. Since the 1930s, parties with lawful access, direct physical presence, sustained funding and the maximum possible incentive have excavated at the claimed location continuously. Summaries report Excavations Incorporated reorganised in 2006 into Kokoweef, Inc., funded by somewhere between 300 and 1,000 stockholders at a 600 USD minimum, with at least eleven individuals reported to have put in 100,000 USD each. Roughly ninety years of motivated, funded, lawful, on-site searching by the claimants themselves has not produced the river. That is not a classified facility's silence. It is a failed search of the strongest available kind, run by the proponents, and it is signed evidence.
propositions.proposed_band: X - VERIFICATION PENDING on my own search completeness; provisional R (R2-shaped) once the excavation history and the corporate/claim records resolve, because ninety years of proponent-run on-site negative results is affirmative content improbable under the proposition, not a documentary absence. If those records do not resolve, F.
supporting: Dorr's affidavit itself - excluded from V under BES 2.5 as self-attesting, since the author is the claimant and the probative content is the claim; routed to ORIG and graded there
undercutting: Ninety years of continuous proponent-funded excavation without the claimed find (search snippets only, from The Mojave Project, PBS SoCal and RareGoldNuggets)
Reported absence of Kokoweef, Crystal Cave and the Peyserts from the affidavit itself - the location claim is an accretion
Reported scepticism that Dorr explored real caves but fabricated the treasure content
propositions.diagnosticity_note: This is the cleanest diagnosticity case on my beat. The BES expected-record framework is built around classified facilities where silence is routine; this entry inverts it. The expected-record profile for a privately-funded treasure excavation is the opposite of the profile for a covert federal facility: the proponents publish, incorporate, sell stock, file mining claims and dig, so a negative result is loud rather than silent. The register should carry a distinct ERP profile for proponent-searchable claims, and this entry is the argument for it.

propositions.statement: The Kokoweef workings are or conceal something other than a mineral-exploration operation.
propositions.assessment: No source I found asserts this and I include the proposition only to close it. The workings are an openly advertised, investor-funded mineral exploration on filed BLM claims. There is no concealed-facility claim here at all.
propositions.proposed_band: X - NOT ASSESSED; no claim to grade. Recorded so the entry cannot be misread as a hardened-facility candidate.
undercutting: Open corporate solicitation of investors, published mining claims, and public site presence - the BES 4.4 minus-D3 cell for any concealment reading
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Included to demonstrate the register can hold a site with a genuine underground void, a genuine legend and a genuine origin document while affirmatively declining to treat it as a bunker candidate.

propositions.statement: The most-cited documentary artifact behind the claim is a letter of 28 March 1975 from Senator Barry Goldwater to Shlomo Arnon, stating that Goldwater had roughly a decade earlier sought access to the building at Wright-Patterson where Air Force UFO material was held and had been refused, and that the material remained classified.
propositions.assessment: This is the fringe artifact on my beat that most deserves careful treatment rather than dismissal, and it is the one where BES's position-to-know gate does the most interesting work. Goldwater is unambiguously real, resolvable in vast quantities of unrelated record, and was a sitting US Senator and an Air Force Reserve major general - so he passes the identity gate trivially and passes a general position-to-know gate as a legislator. But BES 5.4 requires the record to place the person in THE ROLE ASSERTED. The role asserted here is not 'senator' but 'person with knowledge of what is in that building', and by the letter's own content he was refused access - so the letter is affirmative evidence that Goldwater did NOT know what was in the building. It is a strong artifact for a proposition about Goldwater's request and a weak one for any proposition about the building's contents. The related account of a telephone refusal by General Curtis LeMay is second-hand, attributed via a later author, and does not carry the same status.
propositions.proposed_band: X - VERIFICATION PENDING. Ceiling if the letter resolves in a Goldwater papers collection (Arizona State University holds his papers) or in a dated facsimile with custody: A for ORIG. Note carefully: A for ORIG here means 'we know exactly what artifact this story rests on', not 'the story is true'.
supporting: Multiple independent-looking secondary accounts giving the same date (28 March 1975), recipient (Shlomo Arnon) and substance (search snippets only; several are T4/T5 hosts)

A CIA reading-room record titled 'Letter to Honorable Barry M. Goldwater from Vernon A. Walters' surfaced in results - a different letter, but evidence that Goldwater-related correspondence exists in released collections (search snippet only; cia.gov is a .gov host and was not retrievable)
undercutting: Every version I found is a secondary retelling. I located no archival citation to the Goldwater papers and no image of the letter from a custodial repository.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: The letter, if resolved, is highly diagnostic for ORIG and close to null for EXIST or FEAT, because its content is a refusal. That asymmetry is the whole point: a genuine artifact by a genuine, powerful, resolvable person can establish precisely one thing and be routinely cited for a different thing.

propositions.statement: 'Hangar 18' names a specific structure at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.
propositions.assessment: This is where the claim comes apart, and it is a genuinely useful refutation because it is a naming error rather than a factual dispute. The Library of Congress HAER survey records Building 18 in Area B as part of the Power Plant Laboratory Complex - an engine and power-plant research facility whose earliest structures date to the Wright Field era - documented under survey number HAER OH-79-AN with photographic coverage. That is not a hangar. Separately, the Foreign Technology Division, which is the organisation the claim is really reaching for, occupied Building 856, built in the 1970s, becoming FASTC in 1992 and NASIC in 2003. So the folklore's 'Hangar 18' conflates a laboratory building number with a hangar, and attaches to it the function of an organisation housed in a different building entirely.
propositions.proposed_band: X - VERIFICATION PENDING. Ceiling if the HAER documentation resolves at the Library of Congress: R for the identity claim, on a T1 record from a survey with authority over the fact of what the building is. This is the single most resolvable refutation on this entry and loc.gov is blocked here.
undercutting: Library of Congress HAER OH-79-AN, 'Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Area B, Building 18, Power Plant Laboratory Complex, Northeast corner of C & Fifth Streets, Dayton, Montgomery County, OH' (FETCH-BLOCKED; title retrieved as a search result)

propositions.diagnosticity_note: A HAER survey title states the building's identity and function on its face and the survey's issuing authority - the Historic American Engineering Record, under the National Park Service, working with the installation - has authority over that determination. Under BES 3.4 that is a D4-gate candidate for IDNT and for TYPO, and it discriminates completely: a power-plant laboratory complex is not a hangar and the null does not have to strain at all to produce the documentation.

propositions.statement: Substantial subsurface vaults or complexes exist beneath Wright-Patterson AFB.
propositions.assessment: Genuinely unresolved and I decline to close it. A major inter-war and Second World War aeronautical research installation with power-plant laboratories, wind tunnels and test cells will have real subsurface structures - utility tunnels, test chambers, basements - and the claim that 'underground vaults exist' is close to trivially true for any facility of this class while telling you nothing. The specific assertions I found come from investigators who toured the base and inferred a vast system from what they saw, which is interpretation and takes their tier, not the base's.

For a research installation of this age they are expected under every hypothesis, so they discriminate nothing, and a visitor's impression of extent is an interpretation that inherits the visitor's tier.

That is a genuinely resolvable D4-gate candidate sitting under a claim that is usually dismissed wholesale. propositions.statement: The template for an American 'vast inhabited underground facility' narrative - a multi-level cavern world, a hidden population, advanced technology, and a claimant reporting personal experience presented as fact inside a fiction venue - is fixed by Richard Sharpe Shaver's 'I Remember Lemuria!', the cover story of Amazing Stories for March 1945, published and promoted as substantially true by editor Ray Palmer.
propositions.assessment: This entry exists because the beat's job is to trace backwards, and the DUMB corpus is routinely dated to the 1990s when its narrative template is thirty-five years older and has a fixed, dated, commercially published origin. The artifact is a mass-market magazine with a cover date, held in library and fan collections and in the Internet Archive pulp collections; Shaver (1907-1975) and Palmer are both real, dated and documented, with a standing encyclopedia entry in the Science Fiction Encyclopedia. Crucially the truth-claim is documented too: the controversy is specifically that Shaver and Palmer asserted the material was fundamentally true while publishing it as fiction, which is the exact structural move the later corpus repeats.
propositions.proposed_band: X - VERIFICATION PENDING. Ceiling if the March 1945 issue resolves with its cover date and the Palmer editorial framing: A for a template-origin proposition, which is narrower than a claim-origin proposition and correspondingly more defensible.

undercutting: 'Template origin' is a weaker and vaguer proposition than 'claim origin', and it is genuinely arguable that hollow-earth literature from Symmes onward, or Bulwer-Lytton's 'The Coming Race' (1871), is the real ancestor. lineage.assessment: FIVE, and this is the best independence structure anywhere in the sweep: (a) the START verification regime, which produced exchanged data between two ADVERSARY GOVERNMENTS — about as independent as two sources can be, since neither would accept the other's word, and under which the excavation had to remain open for ninety days so the other party's national technical means could confirm destruction; (b) the BRAC 1995 decision record; (c) GSA disposal and auction records; (d) county deed indices for 150+ separate parcels, each recorded by a county for its own purposes; (e) Air Force unit histories. lineage.collapse_or_note: None. This candidate is the register's best available refutation instrument, and the silo beat used it as one: missile fields are the single WORST possible substrate for the deep-underground-network claim, because they are the most extensively surveyed, most thoroughly declassified and most completely disposed-of category of hardened American infrastructure that exists. A live consumer-facing error is recorded rather than a fringe one: former Minuteman LAUNCH FACILITIES in this population were destroyed by controlled explosive demolition before disposal, so what was auctioned at $6,000-$17,800 is in most cases a parcel and surface remnants, not a usable subsurface structure — physically nothing like a launch control facility with its intact capsule, though the two are routinely marketed together as 'missile sites for sale'.

candidates.mundane_alternative: For STAT(destroyed) the named null is A11-adjacent and is worth stating because it is a live folk belief rather than a straw man: 'the silos were not really destroyed; missiles remain emplaced or the facilities were quietly retained.' propositions.assessment: The evidence I have points AGAINST this, which is why it is worth grading rather than omitting. Sources describe the missile stored above ground horizontally under a roof at grade, in 'semi-hard' facilities offering 'limited protection'. That is descriptive prose from compilations, not a design document — but it is unanimous and it points one way.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: This is the beat's most useful diagnosticity lesson. TYPOLOGY(missile launch facility) predicts hardening under the popular reading and does NOT predict it under the actual engineering history of the Atlas D generation. Anyone reasoning 'it launched an ICBM, therefore it is a bunker' has substituted a category for an observation. What would settle it: an AFWL/AFSWC-lineage overpressure specification for the coffin launcher, retrievable from DTIC by report series.
propositions.proposed_band: X — and the projection points toward R (refuted) or a very low band, not toward A. A design document stating a low overpressure rating would be affirmative disconfirmation.
undercutting: Consistent secondary description of the configuration as semi-hard, above ground, horizontal, with limited protection — weak individually, unanimous collectively, and pointing one direction

propositions.statement: The Atlas D coffin complexes were deactivated in the mid-1960s and disposed of; their present condition and ownership are unknown to me.
propositions.assessment: Deactivation is uncontested; disposition is entirely unsearched by me. This is X in the plainest sense — the X-02 shape, not searched and not knowable from what I reached.
propositions.diagnosticity_note: Nothing to assess. FUDS property records and county deeds would populate this cheaply and neither was reachable.
propositions.proposed_band: X — NOT ASSESSED

sources.citation: Astronautix — 'Warren AFB'

sources.what_it_actually_shows: SAW: title and URL. The veterans' association's own page. SOURCE-REGISTRY rates the AAFM newsletter run CRITICAL/P3 and notes it is free, bulk-downloadable and carries first-person Atlas operational accounts — the vernacular record for exactly this question of what the coffin launchers were actually like.

sources.what_it_actually_shows: SAW: title, URL, and summary content describing the coffin configuration, the missile stored above ground horizontally, semi-hard facilities and limited protection. Domain confirmed EGRESS_BLOCKED on a sibling page. Unsourced enthusiast compilation.

sources.citation: atlasmissilesilo.com — 564th and 565th SMS pages

sources.what_it_actually_shows: SAW: domain in a result block. Squadron veterans' association; the preferred route for personnel attestation per SOURCE-REGISTRY.

pair: RES-036 Nekoma Missile Site Radar (the pyramid)
refused_merges.why: Three elements of ONE programme (Stanley R. Mickelsen Safeguard Complex) in two adjacent North Dakota counties, sharing an era, a squadron lineage and a popular name. They are distinct structures on distinct parcels with COMPLETELY DIVERGENT present status: the MSR was deactivated in 1976 and sold twice, PARCS is a currently operating Space Force installation, RSL-3 is privately owned and toured. Collapsing them would produce a single record that is simultaneously abandoned, operational and a tourist attraction. This is exactly the 'two genuinely distinct sites in the same complex' case.

CONTAINMENT, NOT IDENTITY. Oscar-Zero and November-33 are members of the 321st SMW/MG field that RES-046 describes as a population. Merging them would erase the one fact that makes RES-045 interesting — that these two parcels were preserved while the population around them was demolished under treaty. Recorded as a containment edge instead.

Two 'Denver' candidates from two beats that searched blind to each other, one a real earth-covered federal structure with an NRHP listing, the other a non-existent claimed base under an airport terminal 25 miles away. Named explicitly because an automated name-similarity merge would join them and produce the single most damaging record the register could publish.

pair: RES-003 Federal Regional Center, Bothell WA
RES-044 Nike site BA-79, Granite MD
refused_merges.why: Bothell's FRC is reported BUILT ON a refurbished decommissioned Nike missile site; BA-79 is a Nike site in Maryland occupied by the Civil Air Patrol. Shared typology and shared programme heritage, nothing else. Likewise RES-007 Olney, where a Nike installation features in the site's garbled chronology.

pair: RES-013 / RES-014 / RES-015 / RES-016 / RES-017 member stations
refused_merges.why: RES-012 is a SYSTEM-scope record whose extension is exactly the five member stations. It is NOT a sixth site and its sources are literally the same source objects as its members'. It is retained because the chain-level claim (that these five form one programme) is itself a proposition worth grading — but any downstream process that counts six candidates here with independent evidence at each has multiplied one researcher's page by six.

The comms beat caught its OWN search-tool conflation here and recorded it as a finding against its process rather than against a source: a query naming several candidate sites returned the Netcong CLUI entry among Project Office material and the summary presented them as one set. Netcong is AT&T's underground network operations centre in northern New Jersey with no troposcatter role reported; the chain is five mid-Atlantic troposcatter stations. An erroneously admitted sixth member would have inflated the chain's apparent membership and diluted every genuine member's grade. This resolution upholds the exclusion.
Road-name and area proximity only. The comms beat could not establish subject identity and flagged rather than merged. Upheld: proximity flags, never merges.

pair: RES-011 Raven Rock Mountain Complex (Site R)
refused_merges.why: Not a merge anyone proposed here, but the cog beat entered an explicit standing warning that Fort Ritchie, Site C and Site R are routinely conflated in popular accounts, and one of its own leads is a DTIC accession titled for 'Site C'. Carried forward as a standing entity-resolution hazard so a later cycle does not merge them by title similarity.

NOT merged as ENTITIES — one is a site claim, the other a non-located enumeration — but they SHARE A SINGLE LINEAGE TERMINUS and their independent-origin counts must therefore be pooled, not summed. Treating them as two supporting sources for a common thesis double-counts one 1995 lecture. This is the distinction between entity resolution and lineage resolution and it is why the two must be done as separate passes.

Four converted Atlas launch sites in four states sharing a typology, a conversion narrative and much of a marketing vocabulary (see N-20THCENT). Distinct parcels, distinct squadrons, distinct owners. The shared vocabulary is a LINEAGE fact about the descriptions, not an entity fact about the places.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: RES-022 The Notch, Hadley MA — lineage independence
cross_beat_contradictions.cog_says: The wiki family is ONE lineage and six of its members appeared in a single result set; coldwar-ct.com is a probable second; the currency claim rides entirely inside the wiki lineage and therefore has ONE source at any volume.
cross_beat_contradictions.comms_says: 'Genuinely multiple and genuinely independent: USAF/AFHRA records, the college consortium's institutional record, county land records for the 1989 sale, and regional survey work. This is what a well-sourced entry looks like.'
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: NOT adjudicated in the candidate's favour. comms lists only three sources on this candidate — Wikipedia, coldwar-ct/ma, and Grokipedia — and NONE of the four independent roots it names appears among them. Those roots are real and available in principle; neither beat retrieved any of them. cog's count is the one supported by sources actually held, and this resolution carries cog's number while recording comms's claim verbatim. The disagreement is instructive in itself: two agents can look at the same site and differ by a factor of two on independence purely by counting sources they expect to exist versus sources they hold.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: RES-022 The Notch — typology
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Both are correct at different times and the disagreement exposes that a single typology field cannot carry a site with a 1958 military function and a 1989 institutional one. Recorded as typology_historical / typology_current rather than picked.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: RES-022 The Notch — the Federal Reserve currency claim
cross_beat_contradictions.cog_says: Graded as a SEPARATE and much weaker FUNC proposition and separately listed as hollow, with Mount Pony at Culpeper named as the documented alternative referent and a specific FRASER finding aid named as the discriminating test.
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Not a contradiction of fact but a coverage gap, and the more disciplined treatment is carried. Worth recording because a naive merge that took comms's shorter record as the canonical one would have silently dropped the sweep's cleanest specimen of a transposition failure.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: Tier of the Center for Land Use Interpretation
cross_beat_contradictions.comms_says: P4, explicitly, on the ground that CLUI entries are unsigned and carry no citations
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Same source object, two tiers, from beats blind to each other. This is not a small discrepancy: CLUI touches fifteen of the forty-eight merged candidates. Carried as an open source-level question rather than averaged. comms's reasoning is the more specific and is the only one that states a ground.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: Tier of coldwar-c4i.net (Albert LaFrance)
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Second tier disagreement on a shared node, affecting eight candidates. Same pattern: a self-published site by a named researcher, tiered differently by two beats with no contact.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: Whether every launch facility in the Grand Forks field was destroyed
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_a: RES-046 states START I required elimination by controlled explosive demolition of all 150 launch facilities, first in 1999 and last on 24 August 2001.
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_b: RES-045 states the November-33 launch facility in the same wing was preserved — filled with gravel, blast door fixed closed — under an arrangement permitting museum retention.
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Both from the SAME beat, which is why it is a tension rather than a dispute, and the beat named the resolving record itself: the START implementation record, which nobody in the popular corpus consults. Recorded unresolved. A preservation exemption is very likely; 'very likely' is not a receipt.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: Which FEMA/DCPA region Thomasville, Georgia belonged to
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_a: A NARA RG 397 search summary assigns Thomasville Region 4 office correspondence for 1967-68.
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_b: The regional enumeration relied on throughout the cog beat assigns Thomasville to Region 3 for the same era.
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Internal to one beat, which recorded it rather than smoothing it. Carried. Note the enumeration itself is described by that beat as 'the single most load-bearing unverified item in the whole file'.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: Whether a hardened Federal Regional Center was built at Kansas City, Missouri
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_a: CLUI's list of locations where regional centres were built includes Kansas City MO.
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_b: Kansas City does not appear in the eight-member OCDM/OCD/DCPA regional-headquarters enumeration, and targeted searching returned nothing describing a hardened structure there — only FEMA Region 7's current office at an ordinary street address.
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Flagged PROVISIONALLY HOLLOW AND EXPLICITLY NOT REFUTED by the originating beat, and that posture is upheld. A phantom site propagating from one compiler's list is a live possibility; so is a real facility the enumeration omits.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: Floor area of the Netcong / Roxbury underground facility
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_a: Vital Records Inc.'s own facility page: 125,000 sq ft.
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_b: CLUI, the independent surveyor: 86,000 sq ft.
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: A 45 per cent discrepancy in which the larger figure is published by a party that sells storage by the square foot. The self-published figure is inadmissible and anti-diagnostic; the admissible figure is CLUI's, and CLUI does not show its working either. Open pending a municipal assessment record.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: Construction date of the Federal Regional Center, Maynard, Massachusetts
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_a: 1950s / early 1960s / mid-1960s / 1969 all appear across sources.
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Internal spread of nearly two decades on a basic fact about a publicly known federal office. Carried as-is; a four-way disagreement on a construction date is itself evidence about how thin the underlying record is.

cross_beat_contradictions.subject: Atlas silo wall thickness
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_a: The silo-real-estate and silo-tourism corpus: 'almost 10 feet thick', 'epoxy-resin concrete', 'rebar over three inches'.
cross_beat_contradictions.beat_b: Federation of American Scientists: surrounding reinforced-concrete wall about 2.5 feet thick, with concrete at the SURFACE at nine feet.
cross_beat_contradictions.resolution_note: Resolved by the originating beat as a TRANSPOSITION rather than an invention — the surface-slab figure reassigned to the walls — which is why it survives casual checking and propagates so cleanly. 'Epoxy-resin concrete' is the distinctive-error tell that marks the derivation.

citogenesis.claim: 'Western Virginia Office of Controlled Conflict Operations' as an official designation of the Mount Weather facility.
citogenesis.origin: Apparently a coinage of the Mount Weather folklore layer originating with Richard Pollock, 'The Mysterious Mountain', The Progressive, March 1976. No documentary attestation found in any federal record — though the folklore beat states plainly that it did not search federal records for it, which is the check that would settle this.
citogenesis.laundering_path: The phrase now appears as an ALTERNATE OFFICIAL NAME in the PAGE TITLES of both the Federation of American Scientists' Nuclear Information Project and GlobalSecurity.org.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: Both of those sit in this project's own source registry — FAS at P3, GlobalSecurity at P4. A folklore coinage has migrated into the title metadata of reference sites that researchers treat as institutional, which means the citogenesis loop runs through the register's own source list and must be flagged at the SOURCE level, not only at the proposition level. It is also independently corroborating for CONTRA-04's companion finding that FAS and GlobalSecurity share text: the same coinage appearing in both titles is what shared authorship looks like.
citogenesis.test: Binary and cheap: does the phrase appear in any federal record. If it does, this finding collapses entirely and should be struck.

citogenesis.claim: The AT&T Project Offices were built to shelter senior federal officials in a nuclear attack — stated as established fact.
citogenesis.origin: Albert LaFrance, coldwar-c4i.net, who states it as INFERENCE and hedges it explicitly and repeatedly: AUTOVON switching was 'probably not the station's primary mission', the equipment was installed 'to serve another activity', it is 'likely' the stations supported a classified continuity-of-government programme, and they 'may have served' as a relocation site.
citogenesis.laundering_path: Wikipedia's 'Project Offices' article, the CLUI database entries, a Grokipedia mirror, and every downstream retelling (War History Online, OnlyInYourState, realtor blogs, Free Republic threads, YouTube summaries) restate the CONCLUSION WITH THE HEDGES REMOVED.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: HEDGE-STRIPPING is the purest form of this failure: nobody lied, nobody invented, and the resulting appearance of many converging sources is one named researcher's honestly-marked conjecture reflected in many mirrors. It is not hollow as a hypothesis — it is reasonable and may well be correct. It is hollow as a CITATION. The corrective is to restore the hedges and grade the conjecture as a conjecture by a named researcher, which is a real if modest thing to have.
citogenesis.test: Retrieve LaFrance's pages and quote his own hedged wording alongside the unhedged downstream forms.

citogenesis.claim: 'Designed to withstand a 20-megaton nuclear detonation at 2.5 miles' — asserted of InfoBunker specifically, of the Lyons NE station, and of Long Lines sites generally.
citogenesis.origin: A document transcribed as 'Nuclear Design of AT&T Equipment' at qsl.net/n9zia, setting out AT&T design ASSUMPTIONS and an 'Extremely Hard Design (50 PSI)' class. What the page is a transcription OF could not be established — no Bell System Practice number, no Bell Laboratories Record citation, nothing.
citogenesis.laundering_path: qsl.net transcription → Hackaday, 'Horns Across America' (2017) → the general Long Lines literature → individual operators' marketing → data-centre trade press and directories → hundreds of listicle pages.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: A PROGRAMME-LEVEL specification for ONE hardness class applied to INSTANCES whose class is undocumented. The same corpus states many L-3I facilities were designed for a maximum of about 2 psi overpressure — a completely different structure from a 50 psi design. This is the single most-copied error in the Long Lines literature, and its parent document has never been identified by anyone in the chain.
citogenesis.test: Identify what the qsl.net page transcribes. Until then, no instance may carry the figure.

citogenesis.claim: Atlas F silos have walls almost ten feet thick of 'super-hardened, bomb-proof, epoxy-resin concrete' with rebar over three inches thick.
citogenesis.origin: Unidentified first publication — the silo beat declined to name a culprit. Most probable on corpus structure and dating: 1990s marketing copy from the 20th Century Castles brokerage, the entity that both created this market and wrote its first descriptions. Explicitly held as a hypothesis, ungraded, because the dated negative receipt (Wayback CDX over missilebases.com and the pre-2000 corpus) was not run.
citogenesis.laundering_path: Brokerage copy → a Kansas state tourism blog (travelks.com), a travel blog, a UK property listicle (loveproperty.com), an Adirondack regional feature. The wording travels as a UNIT.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: Commercial marketing copy laundered into STATE TOURISM material, which readers treat as semi-official. And it is a transposition of a real FAS figure (nine feet of concrete at the SURFACE) onto a different structural element (the walls, actually about 2.5 feet), which is why it survives casual checking.
citogenesis.test: Wayback CDX over missilebases.com and the pre-2000 silo corpus for the phrase 'epoxy resin'.

citogenesis.claim: Peters Mountain received $61 million of Albemarle County-permitted works in 2007.
citogenesis.origin: The Wikipedia article 'Project Offices', attributing the figure to Albemarle County building permits WITHOUT a permit number, date or applicant name.
citogenesis.laundering_path: Wikipedia → Wikimapia annotation → Grokipedia mirror → onward.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: The highest-diagnosticity number encountered on the comms beat and simultaneously the one most likely to be wrong. It is exactly the profile of a fact that propagates: specific, plausible, attributed to a real and authoritative record class, and unaccompanied by any identifier that would let anyone check it. Albemarle County operates a public building-permit document viewer, so the check is cheap and has apparently never been published. Until it resolves, the honest statement is that a wiki asserts a county record exists — which is a claim about a record, not a record.
citogenesis.test: Query the Albemarle County building-permit document viewer.

citogenesis.claim: An ordinary, publicly known FEMA regional office at Maynard, Massachusetts is a 'deep underground military base'.
citogenesis.origin: Not a claim about the world at all — a restyling event. A Before It's News post of 2015, 'Report: FEMA Bunker (D.U.M.B.) Revealed! Maynard MA'.
citogenesis.laundering_path: Listicle aggregator → state-by-state 'list of DUMBs' pages (coreinsightsintl.com, subterraneanbases.com, deepundergroundmilitarybases.com), several of them post-2022 and unbylined.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: This is the visible, DATED mechanism by which a real building enters the fringe corpus: not by anyone claiming anything new, but by an aggregator restyling a known facility. The transition is a fact about the CLAIM and is gradeable; it says nothing whatever about the building. The structural tell is checkable — the genuine content of these pages is exactly the set of facilities already documented by CLUI and by local journalism, while the added content ('Grey Nest Vaults') attaches to nothing at all.
citogenesis.test: None needed; the artefact is dated and self-evident. Retained as an origin datapoint.

citogenesis.claim: CLUI's class-level sentence — 'close to a dozen sophisticated regional centers… several hundred people for 30 days or more' — read as evidence about individual sites.
citogenesis.origin: One sentence in the Center for Land Use Interpretation's Land Use Database, describing the CLASS.
citogenesis.laundering_path: Returned verbatim in search results for Maynard, Denton AND Thomasville, and read at each as though it described that site.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: Called by the cog beat 'the clearest single demonstration in this sweep' of a class-scope statement being consumed as instance evidence. One compiler's generalisation appearing to independently corroborate three separate sites.
citogenesis.test: Retrieve the CLUI entries and check whether the sentence is per-site or class-level boilerplate.

citogenesis.claim: The Nekoma pyramid 'is now a crypto HQ' / is an operating $500 million data centre.
citogenesis.origin: A single dated act: the 26 July 2022 announcement from the office of the Governor of North Dakota relaying Bitzero Blockchain's statement of a binding acquisition agreement.
citogenesis.laundering_path: Governor's press office → within 48 hours KFYR, Valley News Live, KNOX, Grand Forks Herald, The Center Square, CSi, Walsh County Record, EIN Presswire, DataCenterDynamics → consumer terminus at a loveproperty/lovemoney gallery headline asserting PRESENT-TENSE operation → syndicated onward through Yahoo.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: An ANNOUNCEMENT reported as an ACCOMPLISHMENT, with the tense changing as it travels down the chain. A state press office is a P1-looking source, which is what gives the chain its apparent authority — but the governor's office has authority over its own announcement, not over whether a company will build what it said it would.
citogenesis.test: Cavalier County recorder, and any interconnection or permit record. Against it already: as of November 2024 very little evidence of progress, state funds unused, and a June 2025 company release describing 2.5MW available at a site announced for 300MW.

citogenesis.origin: Grokipedia, machine-generated, mirroring the corresponding Wikipedia articles.
citogenesis.laundering_path: Returned in search results ALONGSIDE the Wikipedia articles they mirror, creating the appearance of two sources where there is one, and the one is already a mid-tier aggregator.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: ALL FOUR BEATS encountered this independently and all four excluded it. An automated ingest counting distinct domains would score every affected candidate as having one more source than it has. Recorded not because any beat was fooled but because the next ingest might be.
citogenesis.test: None; excluded by construction as post-2022 unattributed machine-generated text.

citogenesis.claim: 'Hangar 18' as the name of a structure at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base.
citogenesis.origin: A diffuse mid-century cluster rather than a single text — itself a finding, and what distinguishes this case from Dulce.
citogenesis.laundering_path: HYPOTHESISED AND UNTESTED: the name was cemented in the nomenclature by a 1980 feature film of that title. A movie title propagating back into the nomenclature of a real installation would be a textbook citogenesis event.
citogenesis.why_it_matters: Flagged by the folklore beat as a route the register should trace directly and has not. Recorded here so it is not lost. The claim is separately undercut on the record: the Library of Congress HAER survey documents Building 18 in Area B as part of the Power Plant Laboratory Complex, an engine and power-plant research facility, while the organisation the claim is reaching for (the Foreign Technology Division) occupied Building 856.
citogenesis.test: Trace pre-1980 and post-1980 usage of 'Hangar 18' against the film's release.

cog.claim: 'The 170 Bunkers They Don't Want You to Know About' — a claimed enumeration of exactly 170 underground and undersea bunkers funded through government spending, some large enough to house tens of thousands indefinitely.
cog.origin: An article dated 29 July 2026 on theburningplatform.com, encountered while searching for the origin of the 'Federal Relocation Arc' framing. The article asserts its own basis as 'declassified U.S. government documents, testimonies from former federal employees with top-level security clearances, and investigative journalism spanning over two years'.
cog.why_hollow: The self-description is the entire evidentiary content, which is the self-attestation pattern BES 2.5 exists to exclude: the artifact's probative content IS the claim, so it is not a member of V and is evidence only for ORIGIN. Not one document identifier, accession number, appropriation line or facility name accompanies the count in anything reaching me — and a claim of the form 'exactly 170' is a claim that necessarily rests on an enumeration, so the absence of the enumeration is not incidental but disqualifying. The witnesses are unnamed and therefore fail the BES 5.4 resolvability gate at the first clause. The item is post-2022 with no byline reaching me, which under BES 3.3 makes it POST-2022-UNATTRIBUTED, contributing zero to every condition and counting as zero lineages by construction. Note what I am NOT saying: I am not asserting that no such document set exists. I am recording that this artifact provides no path to one.
cog.mundane_explanation: A traffic-driven aggregation article assembling publicly known facilities — Mount Weather, Cheyenne Mountain, the FEMA regional centres — into a round-numbered list, with the specificity of '170' supplying an authority the underlying material does not have. Every named facility I could see in it is one that appears in ordinary public sources.

cog.claim: FEMA regional centres are 'regional nodes' of a covert deep-underground network, as presented in state-by-state 'list of DUMBs' pages.
cog.origin: A cluster of undated or 2026-dated pages including coreinsightsintl.com 'List of DUMBs by State', subterraneanbases.com state pages (e.g. 'Georgia Underground Bases: 2026 Intelligence & FEMA Regional Nodes', 'Washington Underground: Mel's Hole & Madigan Grey Nest Vaults'), and deepundergroundmilitarybases.com. All surfaced incidentally while searching for the legitimate Federal Regional Centers.
cog.why_hollow: These pages take real, named, publicly acknowledged federal facilities with published addresses — the FEMA regional operations centres at Denton, Thomasville, Bothell, Denver and Maynard — and re-present them as concealed installations, adding no identifier, record or observation to the public material they restyle. The tell is structural and checkable: the genuine content is exactly the set of facilities already documented by the Center for Land Use Interpretation and by local journalism, while the added content ('Grey Nest Vaults') attaches to nothing at all. The lineage is the Sauder/Schneider deep-underground-military-base corpus, which this project's calibration suite grades F with V empty on the ground that the originator is the claimant and the content is the claim. Titles carrying a future-dated '2026 Intelligence' framing with no byline are POST-2022-UNATTRIBUTED under BES 3.3.
cog.mundane_explanation: Search-engine-optimised aggregation over a fringe corpus. The FEMA regional centres are real, hardened in several cases, and entirely acknowledged — they are listed on FEMA's own site, one is on the National Register of Historic Places, and journalists have filmed inside one. Nothing is being concealed, which is why the pages can be assembled from public sources in the first place.

cog.claim: Mount Weather contains an underground city with streets, sidewalks, a battery-powered subway, a lake fed by underground springs, hydroponic gardens and residential apartments.
cog.origin: Traced, and it terminates cleanly. Richard Pollock, 'The Mysterious Mountain', The Progressive, March 1976, based on Senate subcommittee material plus several off-the-record interviews with officials formerly associated with the facility. Every circulating version reaching me descends from it.
cog.why_hollow: Hollow as EVIDENCE, not necessarily false as fact, and the distinction matters. Pollock is a journalist reporting others' attestation rather than the claimant, so BES 2.5 does not exclude him — his report enters V at the D0 unresolvable-attestation floor. The witnesses are unnamed and fail the resolvability gate at its first clause. The result is the citogenesis pattern the model is built to name: a T3 publication resting on T5 testimony, subsequently cited as though primary across some hundreds of pages. I counted eight downstream carriers in a single result set (allconspiracy, moraloutrage, humansarefree, beforeitsnews, usahitman, conspiracybomb, a dedicated blogspot, a Goodreads thread) and every one of them is a copy: that is ONE lineage at any volume. This project's calibration suite grades the claim E with a citogenesis flag, and requires the flag to attach to the PROPOSITION rather than to the site.
cog.mundane_explanation: Mount Weather is a genuine, acknowledged, federally operated facility whose existence is graded A in this project's own calibration set — a 434-acre site with tunnels begun in 1954 under the Bureau of Mines and completed by the Army Corps of Engineers, with a reported 200,000 sq ft of built space. A large real facility with a sewage plant, water storage and dormitory capacity for a few hundred people is entirely sufficient to generate 'underground city' language when described second-hand by people who were inside it and are speaking without attribution. The site's A-grade existence and the claim's E-grade status belong on the same page without contradiction.

cog.claim: There were 75 Presidential Emergency Facilities among the 90 or so Federal Relocation Arc sites.
cog.origin: Attributed in the material reaching me only to 'former government employees', appearing in the Federal Relocation Arc wiki article and its derivatives. I could not trace it further and I record that failure.
cog.why_hollow: It contradicts by a factor of roughly eight the separately circulating and better-anchored figure that in 1984 there were NINE Presidential Emergency Facilities within a 25-minute helicopter trip of Washington, and it sits uneasily beside a third framing describing 'seven locations that would become the core PEFs'. The nine-and-seven figures are reconcilable as core-versus-expanded counts; 75 is not reconcilable with either. The attribution is to unnamed persons and therefore fails the BES 5.4 resolvability gate outright, and under the attestation-custody rule the lineage terminus is the anonymous asserter, not the officials invoked. Note the specific danger: this is a number that would, if credited, silently multiply the candidate-set denominator M in the BES C1c rule and thereby change the grade of every individual arc-site candidate in the register. A single untraced number with no custody must not be allowed to do that.
cog.mundane_explanation: Probable conflation of two different populations that the sources do not keep apart: the small set of purpose-built PRESIDENTIAL emergency facilities in the immediate Washington region, and the much larger set of roughly 90 departmental EMERGENCY RELOCATION SITES across the 30-to-300-mile arc — of which Front Royal, in this file, is one. Those are different things with different builders, different protection levels and different orders of magnitude, and reading the second population's count into the first produces exactly this error.

cog.claim: A hardened Federal Regional Center bunker was built at Kansas City, Missouri.
cog.origin: Appears in the Center for Land Use Interpretation's list of locations where regional centres were built ('Maynard MA, Denton TX, Denver CO, Olney MD, Kansas City MO, and Bothell WA'), and propagates from there.
cog.why_hollow: PROVISIONALLY HOLLOW AND EXPLICITLY NOT REFUTED — I am flagging a discrepancy I could not resolve, and I want the uncertainty preserved rather than converted into a finding. Kansas City does not appear in the eight-member OCDM/OCD/DCPA regional-headquarters enumeration (Harvard/Maynard, Olney, Thomasville, Battle Creek, Denton, Denver, Santa Rosa, Everett/Bothell), and targeted searching for a Kansas City federal regional bunker returned nothing describing a hardened structure — only FEMA Region 7's current office at an ordinary street address, plus two genuine but unrelated underground sites in the region (SubTropolis, a commercial limestone mine which this project's calibration suite grades R on the COG proposition, and the Atchison Storage Facility across the state line in Kansas). The most likely reading is that Kansas City entered the list as a post-1979 FEMA REGION headquarters rather than as a pre-1979 purpose-built CENTER, conflating two different things the same list mixes elsewhere. But a compiler as careful as CLUI including it is a real signal and I will not dismiss it on a failed search conducted with no working retrieval.
cog.mundane_explanation: FEMA Region 7's Kansas City office is an ordinary leased or owned federal office. The area's genuine large underground spaces are commercial limestone mines with documented commercial tenants — precisely the configuration this project's calibration suite uses as its negative control against real bunkers — and their presence in the same metropolitan area is an obvious route for a regional-centre claim to attach itself to the wrong kind of hole.

cog.claim: The Federal Reserve stored large sums of currency at the Notch (Bare Mountain, Hadley, Massachusetts) to restart the economy after a nuclear war.
cog.origin: Untraced. Appears in wiki-family text about the PACCS facility, hedged in the sources themselves with 'allegedly', with no named source anywhere in the material reaching me.
cog.why_hollow: Carried entirely within a single wiki lineage whose members I saw six of in one result set, so it has ONE source at any apparent volume. Its carriers decline to vouch for it. And a documented alternative referent for the same story exists in the same period: the Federal Reserve's Mount Pony facility at Culpeper, Virginia genuinely held shrink-wrapped currency for post-attack monetary reconstitution from 1969 to 1988, and is a calibration case in this project's own suite. A currency-reconstitution narrative attaching to a second, unrelated Federal Reserve-occupied bunker is the standard shape of a transposition. Recorded as a live transposition hypothesis with a named discriminating test — the FRASER finding aid for Federal Reserve Record Group 82, Boston, Box 2644 — not as an established refutation. The separate and much duller claim that the Fed stored RECORDS there is unremarkable and I have no reason to doubt it.
cog.mundane_explanation: The Federal Reserve Bank of Boston used a decommissioned and genuinely hardened SAC command post for records storage, which is exactly what surplus hardened federal space gets used for. 'The Fed kept records in the bunker' becomes 'the Fed kept money in the bunker' in retelling without anyone intending to deceive, especially once the Culpeper story enters general circulation and supplies a template.

cog.claim: GENERAL FINDING, recorded as hollow because it is a claim about the RECORD rather than about any site: that the apparent breadth of online sourcing on Federal Relocation Arc facilities constitutes corroboration.
cog.origin: Not a claim anyone makes explicitly; it is the implicit premise of every aggregated bunker list, and it is the failure mode this register was built against, so I record it as a finding of the sweep.
cog.why_hollow: Measured directly and repeatedly across this beat. On Warrenton Training Center, six of nine results were Wikipedia derivatives (Military Wiki/Fandom, HandWiki, dbpedia, Grokipedia, plus mirrors) — one lineage presenting as six. On the Notch, six wiki-family members appeared in a single result set. On the Mount Weather 'underground city' claim, eight downstream carriers all descend from Pollock 1976. On the FEMA regional centres, one CLUI sentence about the class ('close to a dozen sophisticated regional centers... several hundred people for 30 days or more') appears verbatim in results for Maynard, Denton and Thomasville alike, and is being read at each as instance evidence when it is CLASS scope and excluded from V under BES 2.4. Under the BES 5.1.7 access test the picture is consistent: the sources that could have observed the underlying facts independently — county recorders, contracting officers, GSA property officers, the Keeper of the National Register, AFHRA, NARA — are almost exactly the set I could not reach, while the sources I could reach are almost exactly the set that copies from one another.
cog.mundane_explanation: A small number of genuine compilers did real work — the Center for Land Use Interpretation, civildefensemuseum.com, coldwar-c4i.net, a handful of state Cold War documentation projects, and NARA's own record-group guides — and the visible remainder of the web is derivative of them. The correct reading is that this beat has perhaps five to eight genuine secondary termini and a very large number of copies, and that real corroboration on it lives exclusively in institutional records none of which were reachable in this cycle.

comms.claim: The InfoBunker facility in Boone County, Iowa was 'purpose-built by the military' as a 'former Government Command Bunker'.
comms.origin: InfoBunker LLC's own marketing copy (infobunker.com and its overview page), reproduced verbatim across data-centre directories (datacentermap, baxtel, datacentercatalog, ocolo, cloudandcolocation), aggregator listicles ('10 Largest Underground Data Centers in the World'), and trade coverage.
comms.why_hollow: Every account independent of the operator attributes construction and ownership to AT&T Long Lines: the CLUI Land Use Database calls it 'a former AT&T equipment bunker' with a surface microwave relay tower 'built as part of AT&T's nationwide communications system in the 1960s'; the Wikimapia annotation calls it a former AT&T AUTOVON facility; and it sits within the Long Lines corpus. The claim is also self-refuting on its own expected records: if the military had built it, a MILCON line, a federal deed and a service real-property entry would all be X3 expectations, and none has been produced by anyone in twenty years of the facility being publicly marketed. Under §2.5 the operator is the claimant and the claim is the product, so the assertion is excluded from V entirely and is evidence for ORIGIN only.
comms.mundane_explanation: A common carrier built a hardened equipment building to carry, among other traffic, military circuits under contract. 'Built by AT&T for a network that served the military' has been compressed in marketing copy into 'built by the military'. This is an ordinary and probably not even cynical elision, but it is false, and it materially changes what a reader thinks the building is.

comms.claim: This particular bunker was designed to withstand a 20-megaton nuclear detonation at 2.5 miles — asserted of InfoBunker, of Lyons, and of assorted Long Lines sites generally.
comms.origin: A document transcribed as 'Nuclear Design of AT&T Equipment' at qsl.net/n9zia/Nuclear_Design.htm, which sets out AT&T design ASSUMPTIONS — 2.5 miles from a 20-megaton blast, 1000 mph wind, 40 G shock wave, high-velocity debris, and an 'Extremely Hard Design (50 PSI)' class. From there it entered the Hackaday feature 'Horns Across America: The AT&T Long Lines Network' (2017) and the general Long Lines literature, and thence into individual sites' marketing and into hundreds of pages.
comms.why_hollow: Not because the figure is false — it appears to be a genuine AT&T design criterion — but because it is a PROGRAMME-LEVEL specification for one hardness class being applied to INSTANCES whose class is undocumented. The same corpus states that many L-3I facilities were designed for a maximum of about 2 psi overpressure, which is a completely different structure from a 50 psi 'extremely hard' design. Applying the extreme figure to an arbitrary Long Lines building is the CLASS-scope error §2.4 exists to block, and it is the single most-copied error in this literature. A secondary problem: I could not establish what the qsl.net page is a transcription OF — no Bell System Practice number, no Bell Laboratories Record citation, no accession. The most-quoted number on the beat has no traceable document behind it that I could find.
comms.mundane_explanation: AT&T published design criteria for several hardness classes across a network of over a hundred main stations, a thousand repeater vaults and several hundred unhardened repeaters. A single dramatic number from the top of that range has detached from its class and now floats freely. The correct statement for any individual site is: unknown, pending an instance-level engineering record.

comms.claim: The AT&T Project Offices were built to shelter senior federal officials in a nuclear attack — stated as established fact.
comms.origin: Albert LaFrance, coldwar-c4i.net, who states it as inference and hedges it explicitly and repeatedly: AUTOVON switching was 'probably not the station's primary mission', the AUTOVON equipment was installed 'to serve another activity', it is 'likely' the stations supported a classified continuity-of-government programme, and they 'may have served' as a relocation site.
comms.why_hollow: Not hollow as a hypothesis — it is a reasonable and possibly correct one, advanced honestly by a named researcher who marked it as conjecture. It is hollow as a CITATION. Wikipedia's 'Project Offices' article, the CLUI database entries, and every downstream retelling (War History Online, OnlyInYourState, realtor blogs, Free Republic threads, YouTube summaries, and a Grokipedia mirror) restate the conclusion with the hedges removed, and the resulting appearance of many converging sources is one researcher's stated conjecture reflected in many mirrors. Under §5.3 this is the citogenesis pattern precisely: a hedge-stripping laundering loop, which caps the laundered proposition at E and attaches the flag to the proposition rather than to the site. The sites are real; the buildings are real; the AUTOVON role is well supported. The sheltering claim is one inference, and after twenty years no primary record has surfaced for it in the open index.
comms.mundane_explanation: DoD required AUTOVON switches to survive nuclear attack and specified them accordingly. Every physical feature offered in support of the sheltering claim — earth cover, blast valves, decontamination bay, standby generation, filtered ventilation, remote siting, elevated security — is fully produced by the switching mission alone. The single observation that does NOT reduce to the switching mission is the Greenbrier switchboard reportedly labelled 'CHATAM' and 'HGRSTOWN', and even that establishes a communications relationship rather than a sheltering role.

comms.claim: The Big Hole facility in Chatham County inspired the laboratory in the television series Stranger Things.
comms.origin: Indy Week culture-section pieces ('Is there more to Big Hole?' / 'Does a Secretive Underground Pittsboro Facility Serve as Inspiration for the Stranger Things Lab?'), subsequently repeated by regional listicle and tourism sites.
comms.why_hollow: No production-side sourcing was found — no statement by the series' creators, no production document, no interview. The piece is framed as a question in its own headline. The claim's continued circulation as though settled is a pure amplification artefact and it does no evidentiary work of any kind for any proposition about the facility. I record it because it is the most-shared fact about this site and because a register that ingests popularity will ingest it.
comms.mundane_explanation: A local outlet wrote a speculative culture piece connecting a locally famous mysterious facility to a locally popular television programme. That is the entire event.

comms.claim: The Netcong / Roxbury underground facility is 125,000 square feet.
comms.origin: Vital Records Incorporated's own facility page for the Roxbury vault.
comms.why_hollow: Not refuted, but inadmissible and in conflict. The independent surveyor (CLUI) states 86,000 square feet — a 45 per cent discrepancy. The larger figure is SELF-PUBLISHED by a party that sells storage by the square foot, which under §2.4 excludes it from V outright and, under §4.4, makes it anti-diagnostic: a commercial incentive to state the larger number fully explains the larger number. The likely reconciliation is that the figures measure different things, but that is inference. The register's correct position is that the only admissible figure is CLUI's, that CLUI does not show its working either, and that the question is open pending a municipal assessment record.
comms.mundane_explanation: Gross structural area and marketable usable area are different numbers, and vendors quote the flattering one. No deception need be involved for the register to be unable to use it.

comms.claim: Peters Mountain received $61 million of Albemarle County-permitted works in 2007.
comms.origin: The Wikipedia article 'Project Offices', which attributes the figure to Albemarle County building permits without a permit number, date, or applicant name. Repeated onward by Wikimapia annotation and by the Grokipedia mirror.
comms.why_hollow: Untraced rather than refuted, and flagged here because it is the highest-diagnosticity number I encountered and simultaneously the one most likely to be wrong. It is exactly the profile of a fact that propagates: specific, plausible, attributed to a real and authoritative record class, and unaccompanied by any identifier that would let anyone check it. Albemarle County operates a public building-permit document viewer, so the check is cheap and has apparently never been published. Until it resolves, the honest statement is that a wiki asserts a county record exists; that is a claim about a record, not a record.
